subject: Geography
sub_topic: El Nino and La Nina — mechanism

concepts.name: Walker Circulation: Normal State Baseline
key_dimensions: Direction of trade winds (easterly) and surface water movement across the Pacific
Warm water pooling in the western Pacific and cold upwelling in the eastern Pacific (Peru coast)
Convective rainfall patterns over Indonesia/Australia vs. subsidence over South America
Role of the thermocline depth difference between east and west Pacific

concepts.name: Trade Wind Weakening: The Trigger Mechanism of El Niño
key_dimensions: Why trade winds weaken — feedback loop between SST anomalies and atmospheric pressure
Distinction between trade wind weakening as cause vs. effect (chicken-and-egg debate)
Bjerknes feedback: how initial SST warming self-amplifies through wind weakening
UPSC trap: trade winds weaken but do NOT reverse during El Niño (reversal is a common misconception)

concepts.name: Sea Surface Temperature (SST) Anomalies and El Niño Definition
key_dimensions: Threshold: +0.5°C anomaly in Niño 3.4 region sustained for 5 consecutive overlapping 3-month periods
Niño regions: Niño 1+2, Niño 3, Niño 3.4, Niño 4 — location and significance differences
Difference between SST anomaly and absolute SST values
UPSC trap: El Niño is defined by SST anomaly in central-eastern Pacific, NOT by rainfall alone

concepts.name: Kelvin Waves and Rossby Waves: Oceanic Propagation Mechanism
key_dimensions: Eastward-propagating oceanic Kelvin waves: how they deepen the thermocline in the east
Westward-propagating Rossby waves: role in terminating El Niño and initiating La Niña
Atmospheric Kelvin waves vs. oceanic Kelvin waves — distinction
UPSC trap: Kelvin waves travel along the equator/thermocline, NOT as surface waves

concepts.name: Thermocline Dynamics During El Niño and La Niña
key_dimensions: Normal state: shallow thermocline in eastern Pacific, deep in western Pacific
El Niño: thermocline deepens in east (suppresses upwelling), shallows in west
La Niña: thermocline anomaly is the mirror image — shallower in east, deeper in west
Why thermocline depth directly controls SST and marine productivity

concepts.name: Southern Oscillation and the ENSO Coupling Concept
key_dimensions: Southern Oscillation Index (SOI): definition as pressure difference between Tahiti and Darwin
Negative SOI = El Niño; Positive SOI = La Niña — direction students confuse
Why Bjerknes (1969) linked ocean (El Niño) and atmosphere (SO) into a single coupled system
UPSC trap: ENSO is an ocean-atmosphere coupled phenomenon, not purely oceanic or atmospheric

concepts.name: El Niño vs. La Niña: Asymmetry in Intensity and Duration
key_dimensions: El Niño events are typically stronger in magnitude but shorter in duration than La Niña
La Niña often persists for 2 years; El Niño typically 9–12 months
Why asymmetry exists: nonlinear feedbacks and the role of the maritime continent barrier
UPSC trap: assuming La Niña is simply a mirror image of El Niño — it is not symmetrical

concepts.name: El Niño Modoki (Central Pacific El Niño): Distinction from Canonical El Niño
key_dimensions: Warming confined to central Pacific (Niño 4 region) rather than eastern Pacific
Different teleconnection patterns — impacts on Indian monsoon differ from canonical El Niño
Increasing frequency of Modoki events linked to climate change debates
UPSC trap: Modoki weakens Indian monsoon differently and is sometimes MORE damaging to India

concepts.name: Impact of El Niño on Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM)
key_dimensions: Mechanism: El Niño warms Indian Ocean and shifts convection eastward, weakening monsoon
Statistical relationship is strong but NOT deterministic — 1997 super El Niño had normal monsoon
Role of the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD) in modulating or counteracting El Niño impact
UPSC trap: El Niño always causes drought in India — WRONG; it increases probability, not certainty

concepts.name: Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD): Interaction with ENSO
key_dimensions: Positive IOD (warm west, cool east Indian Ocean) can offset El Niño's negative monsoon impact
IOD is NOT the Indian Ocean version of ENSO — it has an independent triggering mechanism
Negative IOD amplifies El Niño drought impact on India and Australia
UPSC trap: conflating IOD with ENSO or assuming they always co-occur

concepts.name: La Niña Mechanism: Enhanced Walker Circulation
key_dimensions: Stronger-than-normal trade winds drive more warm water westward, enhancing upwelling
Cooler SSTs in eastern Pacific, warmer in western Pacific — thermocline gradients steepen
Intensified convection over India, Australia, Southeast Asia — typically above-normal monsoon
UPSC trap: La Niña does not guarantee excess rainfall in India — spatial distribution varies

concepts.name: ENSO Cycle Periodicity and Predictability
key_dimensions: ENSO recurs every 2–7 years — irregular, not strictly periodic
'Spring predictability barrier': models lose skill predicting ENSO across boreal spring
Role of subsurface ocean heat content (warm water volume) as a precursor signal
UPSC trap: ENSO is often confused as annual or biennial — it is interannual but irregular

concepts.name: Upwelling Suppression and Marine Ecosystem Collapse During El Niño
key_dimensions: Peru/Humboldt Current region: normally world's most productive fishery due to cold upwelling
El Niño deepens thermocline, cuts off nutrient supply — anchovy fishery collapse
Historical naming: 'El Niño' coined by Peruvian fishermen around Christmas
UPSC trap: El Niño warms eastern Pacific not by heating but by suppressing cold upwelling

concepts.name: Global Teleconnections of El Niño: Droughts and Floods Pattern
key_dimensions: El Niño: droughts in Australia, India, southern Africa, northeast Brazil; floods in Peru, California, East Africa
La Niña: floods in Australia, India, Bangladesh; droughts in southwestern USA, East Africa
Teleconnection mechanism via Rossby wave trains in atmosphere (not direct thermal connection)
UPSC trap: El Niño causes floods in South America (west coast) but droughts in Northeast Brazil

concepts.name: Role of the Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) in Modulating ENSO
key_dimensions: PDO: interdecadal SST pattern in North Pacific — warm and cool phases lasting 20–30 years
Warm PDO phase amplifies El Niño impacts; cool PDO amplifies La Niña impacts
PDO is NOT an ENSO-like mechanism — operates on decadal, not interannual, timescale
UPSC trap: confusing PDO with ENSO or treating them as the same phenomenon

concepts.name: ENSO and Coral Bleaching Events
key_dimensions: El Niño-driven SST warming triggers mass coral bleaching (e.g., Great Barrier Reef 1997–98, 2016)
Mechanism: symbiotic zooxanthellae expelled when water temperature exceeds threshold by 1–2°C
La Niña can provide partial recovery window for reef ecosystems
UPSC trap: bleaching is caused by heat stress, NOT by salinity or turbidity changes from ENSO

concepts.name: ENSO–Monsoon Teleconnection: Historical Data and Breaking Down of the Link
key_dimensions: Pre-1980s: strong inverse correlation between ENSO and Indian monsoon rainfall
Post-1980s: relationship has weakened — warming Indian Ocean as an independent modulator
Possible reasons: Indian Ocean warming, Atlantic Niño, shifting ENSO flavors (Modoki)
UPSC trap: treating the ENSO-monsoon link as fixed and deterministic based on older data

concepts.name: Climate Change Impact on ENSO Frequency and Intensity
key_dimensions: Projected increase in extreme El Niño and La Niña events under global warming (IPCC AR6)
Mean state change: tropical Pacific warming may shift ENSO patterns toward more Modoki-type
Uncertainty: models disagree on whether ENSO frequency will increase or decrease
UPSC trap: assuming climate change will simply 'strengthen' ENSO — the reality is more nuanced

concepts.name: Monitoring Systems: TAO/TRITON Array and ENSO Forecasting
key_dimensions: TAO/TRITON: moored buoy array across tropical Pacific measuring SST, wind, subsurface temperatures
Argo floats complement TAO by providing subsurface ocean heat content data globally
El Niño forecasts now possible 6–9 months in advance using coupled ocean-atmosphere models
UPSC trap: India's Argo float program contributes to ENSO monitoring — bilateral/international relevance

concepts.name: Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO) as an Intraseasonal Trigger of ENSO
key_dimensions: MJO: eastward-propagating convective anomaly with 30–90 day cycle — shorter than ENSO
Westerly wind bursts from MJO can trigger oceanic Kelvin waves that initiate El Niño
MJO also modulates active/break cycles of Indian monsoon independently of ENSO
UPSC trap: MJO operates on intraseasonal scale; ENSO on interannual scale — they interact but are distinct
